title: Chapel Corner
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Source row: BARMATRIX Q# 14692 is a Criminal Law / Inchoate Crimes item. The supplied row gives official key B, with answer-selection rates A 2%, B 71%, C 12%, D 15%, and explains that common-law conspiracy requires plurality of agreement when the only apparent partner is an undercover officer feigning agreement.  The pivot is therefore: genuine two-person agreement vs. one real actor plus one feigning officer, matching the reasoning-creed direction to name the load-bearing condition before judging.

Final Christian variation — QID 14692_chapel_corner:

Peter, a Bible-college student, agreed with Paul to purchase illegal stimulant tablets from Paul in order to sell them after a Christian concert near downtown. Unknown to Peter, Paul was an undercover police officer whose only purpose was to arrest distributors of illegal drugs. Peter made a down payment for the tablets and agreed to pay the remainder after he sold them. As soon as Paul handed over the tablets, other officers moved in and arrested Peter. The jurisdiction follows the common law approach to conspiracy.

Could Peter properly be convicted of conspiring to distribute drugs?
call: Could Peter properly be convicted of conspiring to distribute drugs?

choices.A: No, because there was no overt act.
choices.B: No, because there was no plurality of agreement.
choices.C: Yes, because neither an overt act nor plurality of agreement is required at common law.
choices.D: Yes, because Peter believed that all the elements of conspiracy were present and cannot take advantage of a mistake of fact or law.

rightExplanation: B is correct. Peter cannot be convicted of common-law conspiracy when the only other apparent participant was Paul, an undercover officer who was only pretending to agree. Gold Key: common-law conspiracy is bilateral: it needs at least two genuine agreement-makers with criminal purpose. Silver Key: when the stem says “common law” and the other participant is undercover, stop asking what Peter believed and ask whether there are two real conspirators.

wrongExplanations.A: “No overt act” is not the reason. At common law, the agreement itself is enough; no overt act is required. Peter also made a down payment, which makes the overt-act wording even less attractive. Gold Key: common-law conspiracy turns on genuine agreement, not an overt-act requirement.
wrongExplanations.C: It correctly gestures at the no-overt-act piece, but then says plurality is not required. That is the trap. In a common-law jurisdiction, plurality is required. Gold Key: MPC-style unilateral conspiracy is not the common-law rule.
wrongExplanations.D: It uses Peter’s belief as the decisive fact. That is the neighboring unilateral/MPC-style frame, not the common-law frame supplied by the stem. Silver Key: do not let “Peter believed” replace the common-law question: did two real people agree?.

c3.label: CUT
c3.text:
A is cut by the Gold Key: no overt act is not the common-law conspiracy requirement.
C is cut by the Gold Key: it denies plurality, the required common-law feature.
D is cut as wrong-frame bait: it answers as if Peter’s unilateral belief controls.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: B and D fight on one axis: bilateral common-law agreement vs. unilateral belief.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: The stem gives the resolver: common law + only other participant was undercover and feigning. Call B.

studentScript: Common law. Undercover only. No true second agreement. B.

A.signal: The stem asks common-law conspiracy; the Gold Key says common law does not require an overt act.
A.lawyer: Common-law conspiracy is complete upon agreement; the official explanation also notes that payment would likely be an overt act if one were required.

B.signal: Common law + undercover officer = no genuine second agreement-maker.
B.lawyer: Bilateral conspiracy requires plurality. A feigning officer does not count.

C.signal: No overt act may be true at common law, but 'no plurality required' contradicts the Gold Key.
C.lawyer: Plurality is required under common law unless the jurisdiction follows MPC/unilateral approach.

D.signal: Peter's belief matters in the neighboring unilateral/MPC frame; the stem chose common law.
D.lawyer: The defendant's mistaken belief that the other party shared criminal intent does not supply the second conspirator under the common-law bilateral approach.

goldKeys.statement: Common-law conspiracy is bilateral: it requires two genuine agreement-makers with criminal purpose. An undercover officer who only pretends to agree does not supply plurality; MPC/unilateral conspiracy is the neighboring rule.
goldKeys.trigger: common law approach + only other participant is an undercover officer
goldKeys.authority: lawyer_confirmation: Sears v. United States; MPC § 5.03 contrast

silverKeys.statement: When the stem says common law and the other participant is undercover, stop asking what the defendant believed; ask whether two real people agreed.

remediation.title: Undercover partner is not a partner at common law
remediation.signal: Only other participant is undercover / feigning.
